title: Microsoft Fabric for Power BI Users: What Changes and What Stays the Same
excerpt: Transitioning to Microsoft Fabric? AptaCloud breaks down what changes for Power BI users, from data modeling to unified workspace capacity.

toc.text: What Microsoft Fabric Actually Is (In Plain Terms)
The Big Changes: Semantic Models, Direct Lake, and Workspaces
Licensing: What Power BI Microsoft Fabric Changes for Your Team
Report Migration: Do You Actually Need to Do Anything?

html:
Introduction

If you’ve spent years building reports and semantic models in Power BI, hearing that Microsoft is folding the whole thing into Microsoft Fabric probably stopped you mid-coffee. That reaction makes sense.

Here’s the short version: most of what you’ve built still works. Power BI didn’t get retired or gutted. What Microsoft Fabric does is grow around it, extending the platform into territory that Power BI alone was never meant to cover. Your reports still open. Your DAX still runs. But the naming has shifted, the licensing story got more complicated, and if you ignore those shifts long enough, you’ll eventually hit something that breaks at the worst time.

This article covers what actually changed, what’s still the same, and where you’re most likely to feel friction as someone doing real work in this platform day to day.

What Microsoft Fabric Actually Is (In Plain Terms)

Microsoft Fabric is an end-to-end analytics platform that pulls data engineering, data science, real-time analytics, and business intelligence into a single SaaS product. At the center is OneLake, Microsoft’s unified data lake for an entire organization. Radiating out from that are workloads: Data Factory, Synapse Data Engineering, Synapse Data Science, Synapse Data Warehousing, Real-Time Intelligence, and Power BI. That last one is the piece you already know.

The core architectural idea is that every Fabric workload reads from and writes to OneLake by default. For Power BI users, this matters because it changes where data physically lives and how your semantic models reach it.

Worth saying plainly: Fabric is not a rebrand. It’s a genuine platform expansion. But that expansion was built so Power BI features stay accessible to users who aren’t ready to touch the full stack. Nobody is forcing you to learn Synapse Data Engineering just because your tenant got Fabric-enabled.

What Stayed the Same

Quite a lot, honestly. Here’s what Power BI practitioners will find unchanged or close to unchanged after a Fabric migration:

  • Report authoring in Power BI Desktop works identically. Your .pbix files open without modification.
  • DAX. All of it. No syntax changes, no deprecated functions as of mid-2024.
  • Power Query (M) for data transformation inside semantic models still works the same way it always did.
  • Publish to workspace, scheduled refresh, row-level security, app deployment.
  • The Power BI service UI, including the report viewer, dashboard pinning, and Gen1 dataflows (though Gen2 is now the preferred path inside Fabric, Gen1 hasn’t been killed off yet).
  • Embedded analytics and Power BI REST APIs continue working on the same endpoints, with some caveats noted below.

Across several organizations we’ve helped move into Fabric-enabled tenants, the consistent finding is that 90-plus percent of existing Power BI content needs zero changes. The friction that does show up almost always traces back to gateway configurations, Premium capacity assignments, or connectors that were already on thin ice.

The Big Changes: Semantic Models, Direct Lake, and Workspaces

Datasets Are Now Called Semantic Models

Mostly a naming change. But that doesn’t make it trivial, especially if you have training materials, internal documentation, or onboarding guides built around the old terminology. What the Power BI service used to call a “dataset” is now called a semantic model. The underlying technology is the same Analysis Services engine that’s been in Premium for years. Microsoft’s stated reason for the rename is to reflect that these objects are richer than a table collection, and to align with broader industry terminology.

In practice, your shared datasets, measures, calculated columns, and relationships are all still there. The label changed. What’s actually worth checking: if you have automation scripts hitting the Power BI REST API and filtering by object type, go look at those. The API now uses “semanticModels” in some endpoints while keeping backward-compatible aliases in others. Don’t assume the whole surface updated uniformly. It didn’t.

Direct Lake Mode: The Feature That Actually Changes Things

This one deserves real attention. Direct Lake is a new storage mode that exists only inside Microsoft Fabric, and it works differently from both Import and DirectQuery in ways that matter for report performance and data architecture.

Import mode loads data into the in-memory engine at refresh time. DirectQuery hits the source on every query. Direct Lake does neither. It reads Parquet files stored in OneLake directly into memory on demand, without a traditional refresh cycle. Microsoft calls this “transcoding.” The result is query performance that approaches Import speed, without having to stage data into the Analysis Services cache ahead of time.

Storage Mode Data Location Query Performance Refresh Required Fabric-Only
Import In-memory (AS engine) Fastest Yes (scheduled) No
DirectQuery Source system Varies (source-dependent) No No
Direct Lake OneLake (Parquet/Delta) Near-Import No (automatic framing) Yes

The catch is real. Direct Lake only works when your data already lives in a Fabric Lakehouse or Warehouse as Delta tables. If your data sits in an on-premises SQL Server or a third-party cloud warehouse, you’re still on Import or DirectQuery. Getting to Direct Lake means doing a data engineering step first to land Delta tables in OneLake. For teams without a data engineering function, that’s not a small ask.

We’ve seen this go sideways when teams assumed Direct Lake was a drop-in replacement for Import and skipped the Delta table prep entirely. The semantic model falls back to DirectQuery silently in those cases, and the performance gap is jarring when users hit it. Test this explicitly in a non-production environment before it reaches anyone who will notice.

The New Workspace Experience

Fabric ships with a redesigned workspace that replaces the classic Power BI workspace. The most obvious change is a “workload switcher” in the left nav, letting you move between Power BI, Data Engineering, Data Factory, and other experiences without leaving the workspace context.

Workspaces in Fabric are backed by OneLake storage automatically. Every Lakehouse, Warehouse, or semantic model you create physically lives in that workspace’s OneLake partition. For Power BI-only teams, this mostly means the workspace looks different and has more options than you’ll use right away. For teams building toward a full data platform, workspaces become the organizing unit for an entire data product, not just a container for reports.

Admin controls expanded too. Fabric admins can now set workspace-level capacity assignments, control which Fabric workloads are enabled per workspace, and use a unified monitoring hub that didn’t exist in the classic Power BI admin portal. If you’re a Power BI admin today, expect your scope to grow even if your organization isn’t using every Fabric workload yet.

Licensing: What Power BI Microsoft Fabric Changes for Your Team

This is where conversations tend to get complicated fast. Let’s be specific.

Power BI Pro and Premium Per User licenses still exist and still work for standard Power BI use cases. You don’t need a Fabric license to keep publishing reports and sharing dashboards with Pro-licensed colleagues. That hasn’t changed.

Fabric capacity is purchased separately, measured in Fabric Capacity Units (CUs). Microsoft maps these to SKU tiers running from F2 through F2048. Importantly, a Fabric capacity also enables Power BI Premium features for workspaces assigned to it, so if your organization buys F64 capacity, you get Premium-equivalent Power BI features (paginated reports, deployment pipelines, XMLA read/write) plus access to all Fabric workloads in the same package.

The old P-SKU Premium capacities (P1, P2, P3) can be migrated to equivalent F-SKUs. Microsoft committed to supporting P-SKUs through at least 2025, but the direction of travel is clearly toward F-SKUs. If you’re renewing a Premium contract, ask your account team directly about the migration path. Don’t assume it auto-converts.

One practical note: Fabric trial capacities are available at the tenant level and let teams explore Direct Lake and other Fabric workloads without spending anything. Useful for proofs of concept. But trial capacities have throttling limits that don’t reflect production behavior, so don’t benchmark Direct Lake on a trial and use those numbers to set user expectations. That will backfire.

Report Migration: Do You Actually Need to Do Anything?

Mostly no. Which is either reassuring or suspicious depending on how many Microsoft platform migrations you’ve lived through.

Existing Power BI reports, dashboards, and semantic models published to Fabric-enabled workspaces keep working without modification. There’s no forced migration of .pbix files. No required republish. The Power BI Microsoft Fabric integration was deliberately designed to protect backward compatibility for exactly this reason.

Where migration work actually shows up:

  • Dataflows Gen1 to Gen2: Gen1 dataflows still function, but Fabric’s data engineering features are built around Gen2, which uses Spark under the hood and stores output as Delta tables in OneLake. Migration isn’t mandatory right now, but Gen1 won’t see new feature investment going forward.
  • On-premises data gateway dependencies move to the Fabric admin portal, but the underlying configuration is the same. Budget time to retest gateway connections after tenant migration rather than assuming they carry over cleanly.
  • Workspaces need to be reassigned from P-SKU to F-SKU capacities when that migration happens. Admin task, not a content migration task, but it affects availability if it’s timed badly.
  • Any reports using the old “Push dataset” API pattern need a review. The streaming data API surface changed in Fabric and assuming it’s identical will cause problems.

The honest version: if you’re a report author, you’ll barely notice the transition until you actively choose to adopt new Fabric features. If you’re an admin or a data engineer, you have real work to do.

FAQ

Does moving to Microsoft Fabric break existing Power BI reports?

No. Existing reports, dashboards, and semantic models remain fully functional in Fabric-enabled workspaces. The Power BI experience carries over intact, and .pbix files don’t require modification. The main exceptions are edge cases involving deprecated connectors or push dataset API patterns, neither of which affects most teams.

Is Direct Lake mode available to all Power BI Microsoft Fabric users?

Direct Lake requires a Fabric capacity (F-SKU or trial). It’s not available on Power BI Pro or Premium Per User licenses. Your data also needs to be in Delta table format inside OneLake, which typically means setting up a Lakehouse or Warehouse first. It’s a feature worth planning toward, not something you can flip on overnight.

Do Power BI Pro licenses still make sense after the Fabric launch?

Yes, for most report consumers and authors who aren’t using Fabric-specific workloads. Pro licenses cover report publishing, sharing, and standard scheduled refresh. If your team’s work stays within classic Power BI scenarios, Pro remains the right tier. Fabric capacity becomes relevant when you need Direct Lake, large-scale data engineering pipelines, or real-time analytics running in the same platform.

Where This Leaves You

Microsoft Fabric is a real platform change. Not cosmetic. But the Power BI layer inside it was built to minimize disruption for practitioners who aren’t ready to go all-in on the full data platform. Your DAX still works. Your reports still publish. Your users still see the same report viewer they’ve used for years.

The areas worth your attention right now: understand the licensing trajectory if you’re on P-SKU Premium, test Direct Lake in a non-production environment before committing to it as an architecture pattern, and get ahead of the Gen2 dataflow migration even if there’s no urgent deadline. Teams that handle Fabric well tend to treat it as incremental adoption, not a single big-bang cutover.

If you’re framing this for stakeholders, the version that actually lands is simple: Power BI didn’t go away. It got pulled into a bigger platform. That’s usually enough to calm the room and buy you the time to do the migration properly.
